newsitem.title: KENYA: Britain fears Zaire bloodshed unless talks start.
newsitem.headline: Britain fears Zaire bloodshed unless talks start.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and the rebels fighting to topple him must enter negotiations to avoid wholesale bloodshed in Africa's second-largest country, British aid minister Lynda Chalker said on Saturday.
"If the government of Zaire believes there is a military solution they are probably going to preside over the break-up of Zaire," Chalker told Reuters.
Laurent Kabila's rebels control a long, thin strip of land in eastern Zaire and are pushing inland despite the government's promised counter-offensive.
"There have to be negotiations if there is not to be wholesale bloodshed in Zaire," Chalker, the British government's Africa specialist since 1986, said during a visit to Kenya.
"You have got to get Kabila to come to the conference table with whoever is the representative of the government of Zaire," she said.
Mobutu is suffering from prostate cancer and has spent most of the past six months in Europe for treatment.

Kabila says he will only meet Mobutu to discuss the ailing leader's handover of power. Mobutu's government says it will not talk until foreign troops have left Zaire -- it accuses Uganda and Rwanda of actively backing the rebels.
"If (the rebels) think by fighting that they are going to win I think they are in for a very rude shock," Chalker said.
"Because I think Zaire has been equipped, by whoever has done the equipping, to fight them back," she added.

Mobutu's ragged army collapsed when the rebellion began last October. After Zaire imported helicopters, a few fighter planes, weaponry and about 300 mercenaries, it launched a counter-offensive on January 20.
The re-arming and attempts to instil discipline in the army have failed to turn the tide. The rebels are capturing a town almost every day, thrusting west, north and south.

Britain has close relations with both Uganda and Rwanda, the countries showing most sympathy for the rebels. Rwanda has even applied to join the Commonwealth despite its history as a French-speaking former Belgian territory.
France, on the other hand, has been the most important Western ally of Mobutu's for the past decade.
But Chalker ruled out any question of direct French military help to shore up Mobutu's rule.
"What France is concerned about is the undermining of territorial boundaries and I think we would find most countries concerned about that," she said.
